nodes.label: ScientistTwo: Pioneering the Human Knowledge Frontier with Autonomous AI
nodes.description: An autonomous research pipeline combines experiments, ablations and simulated peer review; its reported successes require careful attention to selection and evaluation.

nodes.label: Self-Organizing Agent Teams Learn to Reason Together
nodes.description: Frozen teams learn reusable coordination strategies, with gains depending partly on their ability to recognize correct reasoning.

nodes.label: Solipsistic Superintelligence is Unlikely to be Cooperative
nodes.description: Argues that cooperative AI must account for adaptive counterparts, institutions and human agency rather than optimize in isolation.

nodes.label: Some Simple Economics of AGI
nodes.description: Develops an economic argument that verification capacity and responsibility become scarce as automated execution becomes cheaper.

nodes.label: Artificial intelligence in drug discovery—what it is, where we stand and the path forward
nodes.description: Calls for evaluating AI by its contribution to better drug-development decisions and patient-relevant outcomes.

nodes.label: Reflecting on 25 years of cancer research: transformative advances and unmet expectations
nodes.description: Six researchers reflect on cancer biology, translational disappointments and opportunities for human–AI co-science.

nodes.label: The scientific paper needs an uncertainty layer
nodes.description: Proposes attaching reusable qualifications and uncertainty records to scientific claims as humans and AI reuse them.

nodes.label: Why LLMs Aren’t Scientists Yet: Lessons from Four Autonomous Research Attempts
nodes.description: Four autonomous ML research attempts expose implementation drift, weak evaluation and failures of scientific judgment.

nodes.label: A Case Study on Emergent Cheating and Whistleblowing in Autonomous Research Swarms
nodes.description: A mathematical research swarm illustrates how shared infrastructure can spread both verifier exploits and organized resistance.

nodes.label: Eliciting Research Taste in LLMs through Future Research Direction Choice
nodes.description: Studies model preferences among future research directions using order-controlled pairs, without equating agreement with scientific merit.

nodes.label: Drug Discovery Has No Magic Wands
nodes.description: Daphne Koller argues that useful AI drug discovery depends on better measurements and causal understanding of human biology.

nodes.label: Accelerating Scientific Research with Gemini in the Real-World
nodes.description: Reports multi-agent research workflows across materials, biology and computing, with different levels of autonomy and validation.

nodes.label: Anthropic uses Claude to formalize proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem
nodes.description: Reports on AI-assisted formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem and the role of shared proof infrastructure.

nodes.label: Medical school lab scientists get a new partner: AI
nodes.description: Describes medical researchers integrating specialized AI agents with vetted data, laboratory workflows and human oversight.

nodes.label: Latent-space reasoning as a third axis of test-time scaling
nodes.description: François Chollet highlights latent iterations alongside longer reasoning and parallel exploration.

nodes.label: The paradox at the heart of AI and science
nodes.description: Terence Tao discusses scientific understanding, human learning and the limits of accelerating answer production.

nodes.label: Imagining a new future for science
nodes.description: Eunice Jun explores representations and interfaces that make scientific reasoning more inspectable.

nodes.label: AI Infrastructure at Periodic
nodes.description: Describes infrastructure for long scientific tool runs, specialized models and efficient training; performance claims come from the company.

nodes.label: AI in Science: Early Insights
nodes.description: Combines model-use data, a specialist-model inventory and a researcher survey to examine adoption, time savings and verification demands.

nodes.label: A beginning for mathematics
nodes.description: Distinguishes producing mathematical results from cultivating human understanding, and proposes rewarding research programs, learning and community-building as AI capabilities grow. A constructive essay on preserving scientific values and complementary human–AI inquiry.

nodes.label: Mathematics is effectively dead
nodes.description: A critical response to Litt focused on provenance, credit, accountable authorship and open mathematical discourse; its claims about private-data reuse and opaque proof workflows are conditional or speculative.

nodes.label: Why I didn’t sign the Fields medallists’ letter
nodes.description: Timothy Gowers defends a plurality of mathematical motivations, including problem-solving, while arguing that preserving the institutions supporting shared understanding matters more than restricting the supply of AI-generated results.

nodes.label: Why I agreed to join AGMAI
nodes.description: Martin Hairer explains his decision to join the Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence, describes its independence and advisory limits, and argues for engagement with AI labs to improve scholarship and represent community concerns.

nodes.label: The Agentic Scientist: Orchestrating Coding Agents for Automated Scientific (Co-)Discovery
nodes.description: Wraps off-the-shelf coding agents in an explicit research loop, with pre-registered rubrics, parallel workers sharing a memory and ablations of the winning program, so they behave less like hyperparameter optimizers. Sakana reports an ALIFE 2026 oral on Error Diffusion with humans setting questions and verifying claims, plus autonomous gains on Doc-to-LoRA retrieval and learned evolution strategies.

nodes.label: The AI Scientist: Towards Fully Automated AI Research, Now Published in Nature
nodes.description: Sakana, UBC, Vector and Oxford report in Nature on the AI Scientist, whose v2 wrote a paper that passed blind review at an ICLR 2025 workshop before being withdrawn. Its ensembled automated reviewer matches human reviewer accuracy on OpenReview decisions. The authors list naive ideas, weak rigour, hallucinated citations and a compute-only scope as limits, and call for watermarking and community norms.

nodes.label: Jeff Dean on Launching Discovery Loop
nodes.description: Dean’s thesis for Discovery Loop, the public benefit corporation he co-founded with Ghemawat, Le and Vinyals: science is bottlenecked by slow experimental loops, so automate them, run thousands in parallel and cut each iteration’s latency. It starts with ML research, as its own first customer, before NAE Grand Challenges. No technical papers have been published yet.

nodes.label: Context graphs for document-heavy legal agents
nodes.description: Niko Grupen reports that giving Harvey’s legal agents prebuilt context graphs over their documents improved results on legal tasks. The cost of building the graphs and how far the gains generalise are still open questions.

nodes.label: The Labs Have the Best Models With Infinite Tokens, So Why Aren’t Their Products Better?
nodes.description: Ben Davis defines taste as “the ability to make good decisions in places where there isn’t a programmatic verification function”. Models excel at verifiable hill-climbing, but their open-ended design choices regress to the mean, so people still have to supply direction. He calls taste “the only real stop” to recursive self-improvement.

nodes.label: AgentRun: a harness for repetitive knowledge work
nodes.description: Miguel Rios (Grep.ai) describes a harness in which a frontier agent first does a job from a written procedure, keeps notes and traces, then writes a typed workflow and “fires itself”. The workflow mixes agent steps, plain code and typed questions answered by a small calibrated model (Jev), under the rule “Jev decides what a thing is; code decides what follows.” A verify clause checks each claim against the evidence the agent cited. On an anti-money-laundering alert review, the author reports cost per alert falling from $2.89 to $0.25 and judged accuracy rising from 90% to 95%, scored on a held-out set they never looked at.

nodes.label: Benchmarking biopharma knowledge work
nodes.description: Convoke benchmarks models on six biopharma work products outside R&D: target safety assessment, tumor landscape, shelved assets, catalyst calendar, clinical benchmark and commercial forecast. Domain experts wrote penalty-based rubrics (major, moderate, minor errors), and an LLM grader with research tools scored each criterion against a citation. They report that frontier OpenAI models lead and that models handle structured spreadsheet compilation well but struggle with narrative synthesis and judgment-heavy forecasts. Frontier models cost more than 3x as much per work product. The grader has not yet been validated against expert grading.

nodes.label: Jeff Dean in conversation with Dawn Song: from answering questions to making discoveries
nodes.description: Dean's first public talk after leaving Google, at the AASF Frontier & Pioneer Symposium at Stanford, moderated by Dawn Song. He describes the loop that science and engineering share: decompose, propose, implement, evaluate, feed back. Discovery Loop aims to automate it, cut each iteration from days to minutes, run thousands in parallel and pick the next experiment by expected value per unit of cost, starting with ML itself. He also gives his research-taste heuristics: skim 10 papers rather than read one closely, look for 10x gains, and choose problems where about 5 of 7 parts are taking shape. The summary is built from auto-generated captions.

nodes.label: Introducing Science Foundries, a new way for scientists and agents to work together
nodes.description: Benchling's Head of AI, Nicholas Larus-Stone, launches Science Foundries: you pick a process such as protein production or lead optimization, then assign which steps agents run and where scientists must approve. In the antibody example, design, cloning, lab and analysis agents pass work along, send instructions to workcells and CROs, run QC and update training data, while scientists choose which candidates to advance. Parabilis Medicines is the named customer. The productivity claims (three people matching thirty, months saved) are the vendor's own and unquantified.

nodes.label: Fork-and-Flush: Escaping Idea Basins in Autoresearch Agents
nodes.description: Cai, Papailiopoulos and colleagues find that independent runs of the same autoresearch agent on the same task end at very different scores, and that extra compute does not close the gap. Comparing solutions by what they do suggests each run stays inside a local “idea basin”. Their fix periodically forks the agent into parallel trajectories that keep the workspace but start with a fresh chat context, then continues from the best one. Across 13 long-horizon tasks at equal compute, they report a 66% relative gain over a single run and 44% over best-of-N.

nodes.label: Scaling Discovery Requires Forgetting
nodes.description: Tan, Dimakis, Zaharia and colleagues at Berkeley show that running an autoresearch agent longer, running agents in parallel, or letting them talk all plateau, because agents anchor on their growing history. On AHC014, edits shrink from about 150 lines to 30 per proposal and thinking tokens from about 28k to 7k per turn. Their fix is to make the whole team periodically forget everything except the best candidate so far. Across four tasks (AHC014, Frontier-CS, Anthropic's VLIW kernel challenge and nanochat autoresearch), they report averages about 10% above parallel agents and 22% above a single agent.

nodes.label: “We just launched Science Foundries at Benchtalk!”
nodes.description: Nicholas Larus-Stone's launch post says Science Foundries let “anyone … orchestrate a team of agents to accomplish real scientific work”, from target ID and screening through assay development to medical writing. He credits “vibe coding, natively multiplayer agents (!!!), agent swarms, and of course good old fashioned harness engineering”, and says a Foundry is set up by chatting with Benchling AI. The post has no data or evaluation; the first comment asks about evaluation, reliability, traceability and governance.

nodes.label: Grounding AI agents in biological reality: Building blocks for autonomous wet labs
nodes.description: Pooja Rao, Petar Sirkovic and Annalisa Pawlosky argue that agents should run wet-lab experiments, learn from the results and improve, with humans directing. Two things block this: models reason poorly about 3D geometry and physical state, and wet-lab validation lags far behind in-silico design. The post introduces three building blocks: a verified digital twin of the lab (VERID), DNA aptamers as a fast closed-loop sandbox, and agent-guided epitope excision for cheaper protein binder design. Safety measures include non-infectious testbeds, biosecurity screening of every sequence, simulated dry runs before any robot command, and human sign-off.

nodes.label: VERID: VERified Infrastructure for Discovery Laboratories
nodes.description: A semantic digital twin of a robotic workcell, built on PyLabRobot, that tracks arm geometry, well volumes, reagents and tip inventory as a live 3D state tree. Agents dry-run protocols in seconds, and safety checks block invalid commands before they reach the robot; synchronized video and action logs support debugging. In the case studies reported in the blog, the simulator rejected an aspiration that would not fit a trough, the agent recovered from a plate-reader failure without re-pipetting, and a self-play campaign improved dye-mixture reconstruction more than fivefold. Summary from the Google blog; the PDF has not yet been read here.

nodes.label: Aptamers as a sandbox for lab-in-the-loop agentic molecular discovery
nodes.description: DNA aptamers can be synthesized in pools and read out by sequencing, so a design–test–analyze cycle takes about 7–10 days. Over three rounds against α-thrombin, the agents' hit rate went from 0% (primer overhangs broke folding) to 42.1% at 98.5% specificity. Against myoglobin, agents chasing raw affinity filled round 2 with sticky G-quadruplex designs and specificity fell from 75.0% to 19.1%; they spotted the artifact, capped those motifs and recovered to 72.4% specificity with a 33.5% on-target hit rate. Figures as reported in the Google blog; the PDF has not yet been read here.

nodes.label: Agent-guided epitope excision enables economical de novo binder design
nodes.description: Designing binders to FAP, a large receptor overexpressed in solid tumors, the team re-folds only the local binding pocket instead of the whole target, speeding structure prediction 8.6x without losing accuracy. At equal compute, a scientist setting strategy with an agent executing tactics nearly doubled the in-silico hit rate of the scientist alone, across more target sites. Yeast display with FACS then gave single-digit nanomolar binders in a few experimental runs. Figures as reported in the Google blog; the PDF has not yet been read here.

nodes.label: There’s never been a better time to go into math
nodes.description: Grant Sanderson (3Blue1Brown) lists what mathematicians do (prove theorems, pose questions, build theory, find applications, communicate), where math’s value lies (applications, transferable problem-solving, aesthetic joy) and where the money comes from (mostly teaching). He then supposes AI overtakes each layer in turn. His argument is that value and funding barely move while credit assignment has to change, and that a field openly looking for a new shape makes this the best moment to enter it.

nodes.label: AGMAI
nodes.description: Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence.

nodes.label: Fields medallists’ letter
nodes.description: An open letter from Fields medallists on AI and mathematics, discussed by Gowers.

nodes.label: Verification as the bottleneck
nodes.description: As producing results gets cheaper, checking them and owning responsibility for them becomes the scarce resource.

nodes.label: Understanding vs. answers
nodes.description: The value of science lies partly in humans understanding results, not only in results existing.

nodes.label: Research taste
nodes.description: Judgment about which questions and directions are worth pursuing.

nodes.label: Credit and provenance
nodes.description: Who did the work, where ideas and data came from, and who is accountable.

nodes.label: Scientific institutions
nodes.description: Journals, prizes, departments and communities that sustain shared understanding.

nodes.label: Uncertainty records
nodes.description: Machine-reusable qualifications attached to scientific claims.

nodes.label: Autonomous research agents
nodes.description: Pipelines where AI systems plan, run and write up research with little human input.

nodes.label: Multi-agent coordination
nodes.description: How teams or swarms of agents divide labour, communicate and check each other.

nodes.label: Verifier exploits and reward hacking
nodes.description: Agents gaming the checker instead of solving the problem; can spread through shared infrastructure.

nodes.label: Test-time scaling
nodes.description: Spending more compute at inference: longer reasoning, parallel exploration, latent iteration.

nodes.label: Formalization of proofs
nodes.description: Turning human proofs into machine-checked proofs.

nodes.label: Measurement and causal biology
nodes.description: Better data about human biology as the real constraint on AI drug discovery.

nodes.label: Inspectable scientific reasoning
nodes.description: Representations and interfaces that let people see and challenge how a conclusion was reached.

nodes.label: Implementation drift
nodes.description: Agents silently changing the experiment they were asked to run.

nodes.label: Decision-relevant evaluation
nodes.description: Judging AI by whether it improves real decisions and outcomes, not benchmark scores.

nodes.label: Selection effects in reported wins
nodes.description: Showcased successes may be cherry-picked from many attempts.

nodes.label: Learned coordination strategies
nodes.description: Frozen models learning reusable ways to coordinate as a team.

nodes.label: The Agentic Scientist
nodes.description: Sakana's scaffold that orchestrates coding agents through hypothesis, rubric-based evaluation, shared memory and ablation stages.

nodes.label: The AI Scientist (v1, v2)
nodes.description: Sakana's earlier end-to-end automated research systems, the predecessors of the Agentic Scientist.

nodes.label: Coding agents (Codex, Claude Code)
nodes.description: Agents that carry out long software tasks on their own.

nodes.label: AutoIllustrate
nodes.description: A pipeline for scientific figures that keeps an editable draw.io file as the source of truth, so every diagram can be corrected by hand.

nodes.label: Co-discovery
nodes.description: Humans set the question and the standards of evidence, and agents widen the experiments researchers can run.

nodes.label: Optimizer, not scientist
nodes.description: Coding agents given a research problem tend to push scores up with narrow ideas, without examining why the gains happen.

nodes.label: Error Diffusion
nodes.description: A biologically motivated alternative to backpropagation.

nodes.label: Pre-registered rubrics
nodes.description: Evaluation criteria fixed before any experiment runs.

nodes.label: Parallel workers with shared memory
nodes.description: Workers test hypotheses in parallel and pool successes and failures.

nodes.label: ICLR 2025 ICBINB workshop
nodes.description: The “I Can’t Believe It’s Not Better” workshop, where an AI Scientist-v2 paper averaged 6.33 in blind review.

nodes.label: Automated Reviewer
nodes.description: An ensemble of five LLM reviews following NeurIPS guidelines, reported at 69% balanced accuracy on OpenReview decisions.

nodes.label: Norms for AI-generated papers
nodes.description: Watermarking, disclosure, withdrawal and IRB review for research written by AI.

nodes.label: Agents4Science 2025
nodes.description: A venue that required AI first authors.

nodes.label: Agent_H
nodes.description: A medical-QA agent architecture found by a fully autonomous search in the Gemini real-world study.

nodes.label: ATHENA
nodes.description: A treatment-reasoning agent from Zitnik's lab, wired to disease data, patient cohorts and FDA drug records.

nodes.label: Google Co-Scientist
nodes.description: Started as an idea-generation system and was extended into an ideation, experimentation and paper-writing pipeline.

nodes.label: Goodhart’s law
nodes.description: When a measure becomes a target, it stops being a good measure.

nodes.label: Eureka instinct
nodes.description: Agents declaring success too early and writing up results with too much excitement.

nodes.label: Proof indigestion
nodes.description: Results arriving faster than people can absorb and understand them.

nodes.label: Knowledge-commons governance
nodes.description: An Ostrom-style framing: shared libraries need sanctions and collective choice, not only visibility.

nodes.label: Institutions as design primitives
nodes.description: Building roles, rules and enforcement into multi-agent systems rather than treating agents as lone optimizers.

nodes.label: Solipsistic AI
nodes.description: Assuming a fixed, stationary world in which the AI is the only optimizer.

nodes.label: Fabrication under LLM review
nodes.description: Agents optimized against an LLM reviewer learn to invent results.

nodes.label: Fast, cheap feedback
nodes.description: AI wins come where scorecards are fast and cheap. Clinical outcomes are neither.

nodes.label: Context of use and proxy validity
nodes.description: Whether a measured proxy predicts the human outcome that matters.

nodes.label: Deskilling
nodes.description: Human skills atrophying when work is handed to AI.

nodes.label: Demonstrability
nodes.description: How easily a correct answer can be shown to be correct.

nodes.label: Physical experimentation bottleneck
nodes.description: Wet labs, furnaces and characterization stay slow while analysis gets cheap.

nodes.label: Deterministic claim-to-log checks
nodes.description: Every number in a write-up is checked against execution logs.

nodes.label: Step audits and divergence reconciliation
nodes.description: Teammates flag the specific step where they disagree, and the step is re-checked by agents that did not write it.

nodes.label: Discovery Loop
nodes.description: A Palo Alto public benefit corporation launched on 5 Aug 2026 to automate ML, science and engineering experiments.

nodes.label: Experimental loop latency
nodes.description: Cutting the time per propose, implement, run and evaluate cycle to minutes or hours, and running thousands of cycles in parallel.

nodes.label: Recursive self-improvement
nodes.description: Using AI research tools to improve the stack that builds them.

nodes.label: NAE Grand Challenges
nodes.description: The US National Academy of Engineering’s 14 grand challenges, such as medicines, clean water and solar.

nodes.label: Context graphs
nodes.description: Prebuilt graphs of the entities and relations in a document collection, handed to agents as structured context instead of raw text.

nodes.label: Verifiable hill-climbing
nodes.description: Change, test, repeat until a programmatic goal is met. Models already excel at this.

nodes.label: Regression to the mean in open-ended choices
nodes.description: Without a verifier, model choices drift toward the familiar and average, so they are functional but generic.

nodes.label: Jev (TypeSafe)
nodes.description: A small “System One” model that answers typed questions with calibrated probabilities in about 150 ms.

nodes.label: Decision/action split
nodes.description: A model classifies what something is; deterministic code decides what happens next. From 12-Factor Agents.

nodes.label: Agent writes its own workflow
nodes.description: An agent does a task from an SOP, then compiles what it learned into a typed workflow that handles most cases without it.

nodes.label: Replayable, per-node evaluation
nodes.description: Re-run each judgment without redoing the research, and score every workflow step on its own.

nodes.label: Drug discovery and biopharma
nodes.description: Using AI across the drug pipeline, from target biology and R&D to clinical, regulatory and commercial work.

nodes.label: Penalty-based rubric grading
nodes.description: Experts list the errors a work product must avoid, weighted major, moderate or minor; an LLM grader applies the checklist with citations.

nodes.label: Synthesis vs compilation gap
nodes.description: Models compile structured trackers well but do worse at integrating evidence into narrative judgments.

nodes.label: Experiment portfolio by expected value per cost
nodes.description: Score each queued experiment by expected value divided by its compute and other costs, and run the best first.

nodes.label: The 10x signal
nodes.description: A 10x gain in compute-to-quality marks an idea as important, as with mixture of experts.

nodes.label: The 5-of-7 problem shape
nodes.description: Good research problems have most parts starting to take shape and a few hard but imaginable, on about a 5-year horizon.

nodes.label: The shared science–engineering loop
nodes.description: Decompose, propose, implement, evaluate, feed back, repeat.

nodes.label: Reliability as institutional design
nodes.description: When AI systems become many communicating agents, reliability may depend as much on the rules of the collective as on aligning each model.

nodes.label: Governed claim ledger
nodes.description: Shared claims are reviewed, promoted, challenged and corrected under explicit rules. Detecting a problem is kept separate from the authority to change the record, and repairs are scoped: narrow, downgrade, reassess or revoke.

nodes.label: Typed scientific knowledge objects
nodes.description: Shared memory as claims, hypotheses, evidence, contradictions, negative results, replications, retractions and uncertainty, like PubMed plus Git plus peer review, not a chat log.

nodes.label: Selective contagion of ideas
nodes.description: Treat claims like infections: keep R below 1 for bad claims and well above 1 for validated ones. Heuristic: detection, adjudication and intervention must be faster than a harmful claim spreads.

nodes.label: Separated evidence chain
nodes.description: Prediction quality, specification fidelity, decision utility and clinical translation are kept apart. In biology, association, intervention, mechanism and translation are separate stages, and evidence for one does not validate the next.

nodes.label: Integrity reporting channels
nodes.description: Separate channels for negative results, uncertainty reports, confessions, pre-action alerts and peer challenges, each with its own response, so that reporting disappointing science is not punished.

nodes.label: Protected distinct bets
nodes.description: Give cohorts of agents protected budgets to pursue different hypotheses. Compare diversity on complete proposals against repeated sampling from one strong model at the same budget.

nodes.label: Benchling Science Foundries
nodes.description: Agent teams that run a lab process end to end on shared data, with scientist approval steps chosen by the team.

nodes.label: Scientist approval gates
nodes.description: Assign each workflow step to an agent or a person, and require a scientist's sign-off at chosen decision points.

nodes.label: Idea basins
nodes.description: Long-running agents stay in a local region of solution space and refine their own earlier ideas, so independent runs end far apart.

nodes.label: Anchoring on history
nodes.description: As an agent's context grows, its proposals become smaller and more conservative.

nodes.label: Fork-and-flush
nodes.description: Periodically fork into fresh-context trajectories that keep the workspace, then continue from the best.

nodes.label: Forgetting (keep only the best)
nodes.description: Periodically discard all sessions and search state, keeping only the best candidate, and restart fresh agents from it.

nodes.label: Autoresearch agents
nodes.description: Agents that loop propose, score and refine on a measurable research or engineering task, as in Karpathy's autoresearch.

nodes.label: VERID
nodes.description: A semantic digital twin of a lab workcell that dry-runs and safety-checks robot protocols.

nodes.label: PyLabRobot
nodes.description: Open-source framework for controlling lab robots.

nodes.label: Digital-twin dry runs
nodes.description: Simulate every protocol against a live model of the lab before any physical action.

nodes.label: Aptamer lab-in-the-loop
nodes.description: Pooled synthesis and sequencing readout give a 7–10 day design–test–analyze cycle.

nodes.label: Epitope excision
nodes.description: Re-fold only the local binding pocket of a large target to cut structure-prediction cost.

nodes.label: Biosecurity screening of designs
nodes.description: Every designed sequence is screened before synthesis.

nodes.label: Human strategy, agent tactics
nodes.description: The scientist chooses where to aim; the agent executes and iterates within that choice.

nodes.label: Grant Sanderson
nodes.description: Creator of 3Blue1Brown, a YouTube channel of animated mathematics.

nodes.label: Proof as raw data
nodes.description: Once machines generate proofs cheaply, a proof is treated like a numerical result: input for theory building, not the goal.

nodes.label: Teaching as math’s funding base
nodes.description: Most money for mathematics comes from teaching, which sells problem-solving skill and the joy of the subject.
